title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Continuous
hints: the final array needs n distinct consecutive values. if you keep some subset of the original elements unchanged, what has to be true about them?

the elements you keep must already be distinct (dedupe first) and must all fit inside some window of n consecutive integers, since after replacement they'll be part of a range of exactly n consecutive values

sort the deduplicated values. now you're looking for the window (a contiguous slice of the sorted distinct values) with the maximum count of elements whose value span is less than n - this is a sliding window / two-pointer scan over the sorted array

for each left boundary, advance the right boundary while sortedVals[right] - sortedVals[left] < n, tracking the largest window size found. the answer is n (the original array length) minus the largest such window size, since those are the elements you can keep and everything else must be replaced
commonMistakes: forgetting to deduplicate before sorting, which can overcount how many elements you can keep
using window span <= n instead of < n (a window of n consecutive integers has max - min = n - 1, so the condition should be sortedVals[right] - sortedVals[left] < n)
computing the answer as n minus the count of distinct values instead of n minus the largest valid window size

content.problemStatement:
You're given an array of integers `nums`. In one operation you may replace any single element with any value you choose.

**Return the minimum number of operations needed so that, after all replacements, the array's values (in any order) form a continuous range of distinct consecutive integers, with no duplicates and no gaps.**
notes: all elements are already distinct and consecutive (0 operations)
all elements are the same value (n-1 operations, keeping just one)

sampleTestCases.explanation: the values 2, 3, 4, 5 are already distinct and consecutive, so no replacements are needed
replace 5 or 6 with 4, giving distinct consecutive values like 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 -> actually replace 6 with 4 to get 1,2,3,4,5, one operation
keep one value (say 1) and replace the other three with 2, 3, 4 to form a continuous range, three operations

optimal.time: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sliding window
optimal.space: O(n) for the deduplicated sorted array
optimal.pattern: sort and dedupe the array, then slide a window of width n over the sorted distinct values (a window is valid if its span is less than n), keeping the window that contains the most original elements - the answer is n minus that count, using the range/index relationship the same way cyclic sort problems key off known bounded ranges

bruteForce.approach: for every possible starting value of the final continuous range, check how many of the original elements already fall in that range and are usable, keeping the rest and replacing the others; try all reasonable starting points
bruteForce.time: O(n^2) or worse depending on the range of values considered
